title: Both parties keep the will's freedom
source_text: LVII. Quantumcunque vero tum hi tum illi Scholae Reformatae Doctores efficaciam gratiae divinae exaggerent, nolunt tamen illam quicquam humanae voluntatis libertati praejudicare, sed quaecunque bona opera per Dei gratiam ab homine fiunt, ab iis libere fieri, adeoque primum ipsum actum conversionis non minus liberum esse, quam qui eum sequuntur, nec solum esse vitalem voluntatis nostrae operationem, sed ab ea libere elici.
pass_a_gloss: LVII. But however much both these and those Doctors of the Reformed School magnify the efficacy of divine grace, yet they will not have it prejudice in any way the freedom of the human will, but whatever good works are done by man through the grace of God, are done by them freely, and accordingly the first act of conversion itself is no less free, than those which follow it, and is not only a vital operation of our will, but is freely elicited by it.
pass_b_english: Thesis LVII. Yet however much both groups of Reformed teachers stress the efficacy of God's grace, they deny that it in any way harms the freedom of the human will. Whatever good works a person does by God's grace, he does freely.
So the very first act of conversion is just as free as the acts that follow it: it is not merely a living operation of our will but one the will freely brings forth.
